extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical poetics / literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies Aristotle's criteria for composing and evaluating tragedy (and related poetic genres). Focuses on definition, the six parts, plot unity and magnitude, means of imitation, and the emotional/cathartic function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Est ergo Tragoedia imitatio operis voluntarii studiosi, et perfecti, habens magnitudinem in sermone utili…” (Greek: μίμησις πράξεως σπουδαίας καὶ τελείας μέγεθος ἔχουσης).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy is imitation of a serious, complete action with some magnitude, enacted (not merely recited) in a pleasing language; it must be a whole (having beginning, middle, end) and produce its effect through action rather than description. Evaluation should check that the work fits this definition (seriousness, completeness, magnitude, enacted presentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Six parts of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle’s six parts: muthos (mythos / fabula — plot), ethos (character / consuetudines), dianoia (thought / creditum), lexis (diction / elocutio), melopoiia (melody / melodia), opsis (spectacle / ὄψις).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All six parts are present in a genuine tragedy; when evaluating, identify and assess each part. Note Aristotle’s hierarchy: plot (muthos) is primary, spectacle (opsis) is the least artistic, while diction and melody occupy intermediate roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of plot (muthos)
rubrics_metrics.description: “μέγιστον δὲ τούτων ἐστὶν ... τῶν πραγμάτων σύστασις” / the arrangement/composition of incidents (plot) is the greatest of the elements; tragedy imitates action, not men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well the incidents form a unified, causally connected sequence; the plot must be the driving principle (the ‘soul’) of the tragedy. Superior diction or character-writing cannot substitute for a coherent, well-constructed plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and completeness (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Totum est cui est initium et medium et finem.” / the whole must have a beginning, a middle and an end; beginnings should not arise by chance nor ends be accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the work forms a complete whole: a recognisable beginning (that implies but is not caused by what precedes), a middle (connected progression), and a necessary or probable end. The plot should not start or stop arbitrarily; events should follow logically and form a single complete action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude / appropriate length
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy must have 'magnitude' (μέγεθος); the fable must be of a suitable length — long enough to be complete and memorable but not so long as to lose the audience’s grasp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work’s length allows comprehension of the whole (memorable unity) and fits the practical conditions of performance; avoid plots that are too brief to develop or so sprawling they become incoherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia and anagnorisis (reversal and recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia (reversal, περιπέτεια) and anagnorisis (recognition, ἀναγνώρισις) are chief components of the plot and principal means by which tragedy moves the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating plot quality, identify moments of reversal and recognition and judge whether they are well-motivated and effectively integrated into the causal structure to produce pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters (ethos) must suit and serve the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are part of tragedy but secondary: 'without action there is no tragedy; without characters there may be' — characters must be appropriate and arise from/serve the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge characters by their fitness to the actions they perform and their probability/consistency; good character-writing alone does not make a successful tragedy unless it contributes to the plot’s unity and outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) — ideas and reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Dianoia (thought) is the expression of reasoning, the themes and arguments the characters advance — akin to political or rhetorical content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the clarity, persuasiveness and appropriateness of the thoughts/arguments expressed; check that they arise naturally from situations and contribute to the intellectual unity of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis) — composition of words and meters
rubrics_metrics.description: Lexis (diction) denotes the arrangement of words and the power of language (including metrical composition) — 'diction is the composition of the metres' in verse and the verbal formulation in speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the suitability, clarity, and artistic merit of the language and meter; diction should serve the plot and thought and be appropriate to the characters and genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody (melopoiia) — musical element
rubrics_metrics.description: Melopoiia (melody) is a principal of the pleasant elements; the musical component (chorus, song) contributes strongly to the work’s effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the musical aspects (choral parts, rhythm, tune) for their contribution to the whole; melody is influential but subordinate to plot and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (opsis) — visual adornment, lowest art value
rubrics_metrics.description: Opsis (spectacle) is the visual element — 'spectacle is the least artistic and least part of poetry' though it can strongly affect the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider stagecraft, scenery, costumes and their effect on the audience; recognize spectacle’s emotional power but not overvalue it as an artistic criterion compared with plot and diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis: arousing pity and fear to effect purification
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should 'by means of pity and fear effect the catharsis (cleansing) of such emotions' (δι’ ἐλέου καὶ φόβου περαίνουσα τὴν ... κάθαρσιν).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the tragedy elicits pity and fear in ways that lead to a satisfying and purgative emotional resolution; this emotional trajectory is central to tragic effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of action, not of persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle: 'art of tragedy is imitation not of men but of actions and of a life' (ars tragoediae imitatio est non hominum sed operum et vitae).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work concentrates on significant actions and their consequences (causal sequences) rather than merely character description or moralizing; the plot’s events should embody the life being imitated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means/media of imitation (rhythm, language, harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different arts imitate by different media: 'some use rhythm alone, others rhythm+composition, others instruments etc.' (e.g., citharistic/auletic arts use rhythm and composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the chosen medium (metrical form, musical accompaniment, language) and whether it is appropriate for the type of imitation and contributes to a unified effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of imitation: tragedy vs comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy imitates the inferior (φαυλοτέρων), not wholly evil but ridiculous; tragedy imitates the better/serious (σπουδαῖα).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify the work’s object of imitation correctly and judge whether comic or tragic modes are employed consistently and appropriately to the object (ridiculous vs serious).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of presentation: acting (drama) vs narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation may be presented 'as if performed' (acted) or by narrative/recitation; some works mix modes (acting + narration), and poets vary in which they employ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, note whether the piece presents events through enacted scenes or narrated report, and whether the chosen mode suits the plot and emotional aims (e.g., enacted situations more effective for pity/fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement and causal necessity of incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents must be arranged not by chance but by necessity or probability; the sequence must follow from causes and be sensibly ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the causal logic: are events motivated, do they follow plausibly, and do they lead to the necessary or probable conclusion? Avoid plots with arbitrary beginnings/ends or disconnected episodes.
